This piece of functional art is here to remind you that no matter how gloopy and messy life gets, there is always love and joy bursting through. 🌈💗 I am so excited to finally start sharing the first pieces from my 2026 collection! The first half of this year has been full of learning, experimenting, and pushing my work in new directions. It has also been one of the heaviest seasons of my life. While making this collection, I found myself returning again and again to the same idea: choosing hope. This piece feels like a little celebration of that. A reminder that even when things feel overwhelming, beautiful things can still emerge from the mess. Thankfully, the scary chapter my chosen family has been living through is coming to a very happy ending, and I am sitting in deep gratitude for that. Not everyone gets that outcome, and I don’t take it for granted for a second. So tell me, what makes you stay hopeful when life feels extra gloopy? #ceramicartist #dopaminedecor #glitterinlay #rainbowart #processvideo

How to build a pot using the slab technique. 1. Prepare the slabs:  Take a ball or cube of clay, start flattening it using your hands at first and then a rolling pin To achieve an even thickness I use wooden guides (like in the video). Once ready, cut a circle for the base and a rectangle for the side wall 2. Assemble and cut to measure: Place the rectangle all the way around on top of the base and let the ends overlap. With a sharp knife cut through both overlapping ends with a single cut. This will ensure the sides will close perfectly.  3. Score and Slip:  To bind pieces of clay together it’s essential to score and slip both surfaces. Scoring means making little marks with a needle or a scoring tool to make the surface “rough”. The Slip is simply very watery clay that has the consistently of a paste and acts as glue.  Note: it’s important we do this both to attach the two ends of the side wall and also the walls to the base. 4. Smooth Once all elements are bound together it’s time to smooth out all imperfections  5. videos.caption: I’m a sucker for the making of pots, the joyous throwing and trimming, but what comes after, the waxing, glazing and firing, is more of a laborious task that normally ends up being highly repetitive. I don’t mind the work, I keep my headphones on and listen to stories throughout the day, yet I definitely experience more pain in my hands from these processes, as compared to throwing and trimming. Specifically, it’s the grasping of pots as I fettle the surface clean, as the fingers that are gripped so tightly around the object cannot move, otherwise they rub down the surface and create thin patches that show in the finished pots. This means that the hand that holds the pots is tensed for hours on end with my fingers pressed against a relatively powdery surface, if I squeeze too hard, the clay can fracture and come off of the vessel and too loose a grip means my digits glide across the surface, again creating thin spots. It’s hard to describe, but essentially this hand becomes a vice whilst the other carefully cleans the surface. It’s a skill, just like any other in the making process. #pottery #glazing #glaze #howto #craftsmanship #ceramics

If you’d like to see a far more thorough exploration of these vases, I recommend watching the 40-minute version that’s on my YouTube channel, a link to which you can find via the Linktree in my profile’s biography.   This week I’m making some of my favourite pots, they aren’t really about function, at least that is not what I’m thinking about whilst I create them. These angular vases with a protruding line across one side are simple, decorative objects and a welcome change after a few weeks of focusing solely on functional ware. I take my time with them and pay close attention to proportion and surface and how the line travels and over the past few years they’ve changed quite a lot.   They used to appear squatter and the lines were heavier and less defined but after making many batches, they have gradually become taller and more refined, in my opinion. The carved line has followed that shift, it’s sharper now, more deliberate and despite only being a relatively small addition, the change it makes is drastic. Most of my work is thrown on the wheel and naturally symmetrical and therefore this detail interrupts that uniformity. It gives the vessel a direction and a front. It catches the light and throws a shadow across the flat planes and somehow that single line makes the pots feel more figurative, especially when they are grouped together.   If you happen to click over and watch the longer edition, thank you, it means so much!   #pottery #vase #sculpture #handmade #ceramics

videos.caption:
How to use Hot Wax when Dipping Pots: 
 .
 Follow these step-by-step instructions:
 .
 Ensure adequate ventilation and take necessary precautions to prevent burns. Begin by melting natural candle wax until it reaches a fluid state (if it fumes turn heat down until fuming stops) then continue to maintain that optimal temperature throughout the process. It's worth noting that the candle wax we employ will burn off and vaporize in the glaze kiln at a low temperature.
 .
 Now, place your pots in a frying pan, carefully rotating them to achieve even coverage. Pay particular attention to the bases and feet of your pottery, taking care to avoid any wax drips that may require subsequent removal through sanding or refiring in a bisque kiln.
 .
 After the hot wax has solidified, proceed to thoroughly mix your glaze batch. Utilize a high-speed mixer to blend and suspend all glaze ingredients in a bucket, ensuring a consistent and well-homogenised mixture.
 .
 Next comes the crucial step of dipping your pottery pieces into the glaze bucket. As you immerse the wax-coated pottery into the glaze, ensure full coverage of both waxed and unsealed areas. Observe how the glaze effortlessly slides off the wax and back into the bucket, creating clean lines. This technique establishes distinct boundaries between the glazed and unglazed sections, with the unglazed areas serving the purpose of preventing the pot from adhering to the kiln shelf.
 .
 Remember to stir the glaze in between each dip, using a whisk to prevent settling and the formation of water on the surface. Glaze consistency can change rapidly, so frequent mixing is essential to maintain optimal results.
 .
 By following these guidelines, you'll unlock the potential of hot waxing, a helpful technique used by many potters.
 
 .
 Happy Potting to you!  😀
